rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-peak elution window while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. Moderate temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction once the critical pairs are identified.

The first pair is the only resolution bottleneck, while the last peak already elutes before 10 minutes. Keeping the gradient unchanged and raising temperature tests whether temperature-dependent selectivity can resolve this pair without adding a time penalty.

At 60 C only the first pair remains slightly below baseline resolution. Lengthening the gradient by one grid step tests whether a shallower slope lifts its resolution above 1.5 while keeping the last peak comfortably within 10 minutes.
Injection 3 attained the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Shift the gradient window upward while preserving its slope to test whether all peaks can elute sooner without losing full resolution.

Restore the lower starting organic fraction to improve separation of the first pair, using a slope between those of injections 2 and 3. This should retain full resolution while bringing the last peak out sooner than the maximum-score benchmark.

Narrow the gradient window and shorten its duration, making the slope only slightly steeper than injection 5. The endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution fraction, so this tests a faster method while aiming to preserve R >= 1.5 for every pair.

A slightly steeper gradient tests the first pair’s full-resolution boundary while shortening the programmed ramp. The last peak will likely elute during the final hold; this run tests whether that hold preserves an overall elution time below 10 minutes.

With the maximum CRF secured, test a cooler, steeper gradient for a potentially faster fully resolved method. The strong temperature response of the first pair may reflect an elution-order crossover, in which case cooling could open a useful alternative selectivity window.

Cooling resolved the first pair but created a late three-peak cluster. Raise temperature by one step with the gradient unchanged to test whether that cluster separates while the first pair retains sufficient resolution.

Raise temperature to spread the late cluster and increase the starting organic fraction to shorten retention. This tests whether the shifted solvent window preserves the cooler-temperature separation of the first pair, opening a faster alternative to the 60 C methods.

Return to the successful 60 C selectivity and test a slope just steeper than injection 7. This brackets the first pair’s R = 1.5 boundary and may reduce the last-peak time while preserving the maximum CRF.

Injection 11 brackets the slope limit at the lowest starting organic fraction. Test a slightly shallower version of injection 4 to recover full resolution with a higher starting fraction and establish an alternative maximum-score method.

Test whether a steeper gradient breaks up the late three-peak cluster seen at 25 C, where the first pair had resolution to spare. Changing only gradient duration isolates slope-dependent selectivity and explores a faster alternative to the fully resolved 60 C methods.

The late cluster barely responded to gradient duration at 25 C, so test a shifted solvent window at 30 C instead. A higher starting fraction offsets the shallower slope’s time cost while probing whether both the early and late critical pairs can reach full resolution.

Raise only temperature from injection 14 to improve the remaining late critical pair and shorten retention. This tests whether the first pair’s resolution margin is sufficient to yield another fully resolved selectivity window.

Refine the successful higher-starting-organic method with a slope of 0.0708 per minute, between injections 12 and 4. This tests the fastest fully resolved boundary at phi0 = 0.10 while keeping the maximum-score methods already established.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to compensate for the first pair’s loss of resolution. This probes whether further window trimming can match full resolution and improve on the approximately seven-minute elution time.

Return to the low starting fraction and the slope that gave R = 1.67 in injection 3, trimming the endpoint to just above the last peak’s estimated elution fraction. This targets the maximum CRF with more resolution margin than injection 7 and a shorter programmed gradient than injection 3.

At 35 C the late critical pairs separate, but the first pair needs a lower starting fraction and shallower slope. Test those adjustments together to seek a fully resolved, lower-temperature alternative with the last peak still expected before 10 minutes.

Keep the slope close to injection 19 while raising the endpoint so the last compound elutes during the gradient rather than the hold. This should remove the small time penalty while preserving full resolution at 35 C.

The maximum CRF is already secured, with injection 7 the fastest fully resolved method observed. Test a shallower gradient to increase the critical-pair resolution margin while aiming to keep every peak within 10 minutes.

Preserve injection 21’s slope while raising the starting organic fraction to shorten elution and improve the middle critical pair. The first pair will likely lose some resolution, but the existing margin may allow a faster maximum-score method with more separation margin than injection 7.

Steepen injection 21 by one endpoint step to shorten elution while retaining substantial resolution margin for both critical pairs. This targets a maximum-score compromise between the fastest method in injection 7 and the better-separated method in injection 21.

Increase the endpoint one step from injection 23 to shorten retention while preserving a useful resolution margin. The resulting slope lies between two fully resolved methods, so all eight peaks should remain resolved and elute before 10 minutes.

Increase the endpoint one step from injection 24 to shorten elution while retaining full resolution; this slope previously achieved a minimum R of 1.67. The maximum CRF is already secured, and injection 7 remains the fastest fully resolved method observed.
